property_summary: After any external address calls transferOwnership, the owner must always remain the caller unless the caller was already the owner; the mutant allows any non-owner to become owner, violating this invariant.
After any call to transferOwnership, the owner must remain unchanged or only change to the caller if the caller was the previous owner; the mutant allows a non-owner caller to become the new owner.
After any call to transferOwnership, if the caller is not the current owner, the owner must remain unchanged; the buggy version allows any caller to change owner to any address.

For any caller, after transferOwnership(newOwner) the owner remains the caller if the caller was the original owner; otherwise the owner must stay unchanged — the bug lets a non-owner caller become the new owner with any address.
After any call to transferOwnership, owner should remain unchanged if the caller is not the current owner; the bug allows any caller to change owner, violating this access-control invariant.
For any address newOwner and any caller, after transferOwnership(newOwner) on C, if the caller is not the current owner, the owner must remain unchanged; the bug permits any caller to change owner.
After any call to transferOwnership by the current owner, the owner state variable must equal the passed newOwner argument; the buggy version leaves the owner unchanged, violating this rule.
After any call to transferOwnership, the owner must be the newly transferred address; the buggy version violates this by always setting owner to msg.sender.
After a successful transferOwnership call by the current owner, the owner must be the newOwner argument; the mutant incorrectly sets it to msg.sender.
For any call to transferOwnership by the current owner, the resulting owner must equal the _newOwner argument; the bug sets owner to msg.sender instead.
After any valid call to transferOwnership, the owner should be the address passed as argument; the bug sets owner to address(0) instead.
After transferOwnership completes, owner should not be the zero address, unless it was deliberately set; the bug always makes owner address(0), violating this invariant for any non-zero newOwner.

For any non-zero newOwner, after a successful transferOwnership call, the owner should equal the newOwner argument; the bug always sets owner to address(0), so the owner never matches the supplied newOwner.
After any call to transferOwnership by the current owner, the owner remains the same as before the call; the bug changes owner to address(0), breaking this preservation.

After a successful call to transferOwnership, the next call to transferOwnership from the same owner must succeed; the bug sets owner to address(0), so the original owner can never call transferOwnership again (onlyOwner reverts).
Any address can successfully call transferOwnership after the modifier is removed, whereas in the reference only the current owner can change the owner.

For any caller, after a successful call to transferOwnership, the new owner address reported by owner() must equal the address passed as the new owner argument; the bug (removing onlyOwner) does not break this property in the same way as it breaks access control—instead, focus on the fact that only the current owner should be able to invoke transferOwnership and the call should succeed, so the property is that any non-owner caller must cause the call to fail, which the bug violates by allowing non-owner callers to change ownership.
Any call to transferOwnership by a caller that is not the current owner must revert; the bug removes the onlyOwner check so a non-owner can successfully change the owner.

For any caller, after calling owned() on both reference and mutant, the owner remains unchanged, but the mutant's owned() succeeds without onlyOwner check, violating the invariant that non-owner calls must revert.
Any call to owned() through the reference C must revert when not called by the owner, but the mutant allows it to succeed, so a non-owner can execute owned() without revert.
